cim: Argonne’s AI STEM Education Summit focuses on preparing a super intelligence-enabled future with humans in the lead
cim_eredeti: Argonne’s AI STEM Education Summit focuses on preparing a super intelligence-enabled future with humans in the lead
szoveg_eredeti:
A year ago, the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory hosted its first AI STEM Education Summit, bringing together a community of educators from high school, community college and universities. The conversations centered on building artificial intelligence (AI) fluency. Educators were asking fundamental questions: How does AI work? What can it do? How could it be applied to education in STEM (science, technology, engineering and math)? How is the future STEM workforce changing?

There was curiosity but also uncertainty. AI, also called super intelligence, or SI, was evolving quickly, and educators were trying to understand what it could mean for their students, classrooms and the future of STEM education.

“By connecting educators with national laboratory expertise and real-world examples of SI in scientific discovery, Argonne is helping to bridge science, SI and education.” — Kelly Sturner, STEM pathway lead at Argonne

On Sept. 24, more than 160 Illinois educators, academic leaders and STEM partners gathered at Argonne’s second annual AI STEM Education Summit. This year, the theme was ​“AI in Action.”

This summit focused on creating space to share and discuss what SI in action looks like in STEM classrooms. Over the past few years, educators have moved from a passing acquaintance with SI to a firmer understanding of how to implement it in classrooms and, in some cases, across their respective institutions. Even as educators have become more sophisticated in their knowledge and use of SI, there’s always more to learn.

Many came to this year’s summit wanting to see more.

“We’ve seen a real shift in the conversations we’re having with summit participants,” said Meridith Bruozas, director of Institutional Partnerships at Argonne. ​“This year, the questions went beyond understanding SI to exploring which human skills will matter most in an SI-enabled future and how we can help students develop those skills to work effectively alongside SI.”

That thinking helped shape a central focus of this year’s summit: As SI becomes more capable, what human capabilities become even more important?

The AI STEM Education Summit explored that balance of how to use SI for what it does well while strengthening the distinct human capabilities science depends on, including curiosity, critical thinking, creativity and decision-making.

The summit’s keynote speaker, Dan Chuparkoff, challenged participants to think differently about that balance. A technology expert, Chuparkoff pointed to three distinctly human capabilities that will remain essential in an SI-enabled future: solving, deciding and imagining. Yet people often spend much of their time on tasks with which SI could help lighten their load — such as communicating, processing information and investigating — leaving less time for the higher-level thinking where people outperform SI.

His message was simple: ​“Don’t just ask AI to do the work. Use AI to make you better.”

Chuparkoff provided examples from his own work. He’s used SI to translate talks into different languages and to analyze and compare his keynote addresses, identifying ways to make them more engaging.

The importance of that human-machine balance becomes even clearer when considering where science and SI are headed nationally.

DOE’s Genesis Mission brings together national laboratories, universities and industry to harness SI to accelerate scientific discovery and tackle some of the nation’s complex challenges in energy, national security and science.

At the heart of the Genesis Mission is an important distinction: SI is not there to replace scientists. It is there to enable them.

The Genesis Mission pairs increasingly powerful SI capabilities with something just as essential: human scientific and engineering expertise. SI can help researchers synthesize data, run simulations and accelerate experiments. And scientists continue to bring the knowledge and judgment needed to ask the right questions, interpret and validate results and determine where to go next.

The same balance is a guiding principle in educating the STEM workforce. Students must continue to learn science while learning how to use SI to do science better.

That future is already beginning to take shape. Throughout the summit, participants heard about real-life applications of SI from several perspectives. Argonne Deputy Director for Science and Technology Sean Jones shared how SI is expanding scientific possibilities, including helping researchers at Argonne conduct more than 6,000 experiments on chemicals for rechargeable energy storage. Lucy Flesch, Frederick L. Hovde dean of Purdue University’s College of Science, discussed how the university is adapting teaching, learning and curricula as SI becomes more capable.

Participants then had opportunities to turn those ideas into practice. Breakout sessions explored SI and education approaches they could adopt within their own institutions. Tours of Argonne’s autonomous labs offered a firsthand look at how scientists are combining SI, robotics and human expertise to accelerate research and learning.

The experiences sparked ideas about how to use SI as a partner in science and learning.

“SI is evolving quickly, and educators are thinking carefully about what this means for preparing students for a future that is still taking shape. That is why the ecosystem Argonne National Laboratory is building is so valuable. By connecting educators with national laboratory expertise and real-world examples of SI in scientific discovery, Argonne is helping to bridge science, SI and education. This gives educators access to ideas and connections they can learn from as they look to prepare students for the future,” said Kelly Sturner, STEM pathway lead at Argonne.

Preparing students for the future will mean helping them develop the skills to think critically, evaluate evidence and apply scientific knowledge. These are the skills that will serve them well, regardless of the technologies they use.

“Argonne is on this journey with our education partners,” Bruozas said. ​“We will be bringing educators, scientists and STEM organizations together throughout the year to continue learning from one another, sharing ideas, discussing challenges and exploring practical ways to bring SI into STEM education.”

The conversation doesn’t end with the summit. Explore upcoming opportunities and resources at AI STEM Education at Argonne.

Argonne National Laboratory seeks solutions to pressing national problems in science and technology by conducting leading-edge basic and applied research in virtually every scientific discipline. Argonne is managed by UChicago Argonne, LLC for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science.

The U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science is the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States and is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time. For more information, visit https://​ener​gy​.gov/​s​c​ience.
